nameStory: Tea viburnum gets its name from its native China, where the leaves were traditionally used to make herbal tea. The species name 'setigerum' means 'bearing bristles,' referring to the tiny bristle-like hairs found on various parts of the plant. This Asian native was brought to North America as an ornamental shrub and occasionally escapes cultivation.
description: Tea viburnum is a deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall with an open, somewhat loose branching pattern. It's an Asian native that's occasionally found naturalized in New England, though it remains quite rare here. The shrub produces clusters of small white flowers in late spring, followed by bright red berries that eventually turn black. Its leaves are oval-shaped with prominent veining and turn attractive colors in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Bright red oval berries in drooping clusters that gradually turn black as they ripen - the berries often persist into winter and feel slightly soft when ripe

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long with prominent parallel veins running from the midrib to the leaf edge - leaves feel slightly rough and have tiny bristly hairs

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers in flat-topped clusters about 3-4 inches across in late May to early June - flowers have a mild, slightly sweet fragrance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Open, somewhat irregular shrub form with arching branches that can look a bit wild or unkempt compared to other viburnums

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray-brown bark on younger stems with small raised dots (lenticels) - older stems develop shallow grooves

habitat: Tea viburnum is primarily found as an escaped ornamental plant in suburban and urban areas of New England, often near old home sites or abandoned gardens. It occasionally naturalizes in forest edges, thickets, and disturbed areas with well-drained soil. Look for it in areas where other non-native shrubs have established themselves.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late April to early May, followed by clusters of creamy-white flowers in late May to early June that attract various small pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Green berries develop and gradually ripen to bright red by late summer - the oval leaves remain green and provide good identifying features.
seasonality.fall: Berries turn from red to dark purple-black and leaves may turn yellow to reddish-purple before dropping, though fall color can be variable.
seasonality.winter: Dark berries often persist on bare branches into winter, and the smooth bark with small raised dots becomes more visible for identification.

funFact: Tea viburnum berries change color like a traffic light - starting green, turning bright red, then finally deep purple-black when fully ripe, and birds often prefer them at different stages of this color transformation!
confusionNotes: Tea viburnum can be confused with other red-berried viburnums like guelder-rose, but tea viburnum's berries are oval rather than round and turn black when fully ripe. The leaves also have more prominent parallel veining than most other viburnums.
contextualKnowledge: As a non-native species from China, tea viburnum is much less common in New England than our native viburnums, with only 19 recorded observations. Gardeners sometimes plant it for its ornamental berries, but it's not as hardy or well-adapted as native species like hobblebush or arrowwoods.
compareHints: Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods. Its leaves also have more distinctly parallel veining compared to the more varied leaf shapes of hobblebush or mapleleaf viburnum. The overall growth habit is more open and irregular than the denser, more compact native viburnums.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
